title: 'I feared for my life' officer tells inquest
article: The officer who shot and killed a knife-wielding break-in suspect, had no other choice but to fire, an Aurora inquest heard Tuesday.It was 4:16 p.m. Sept. 7, 2006 when York Regional Police Const. Jeff Biersteker was called to a break and enter on Southwind Court in Newmarket.What the call developed into was something the officer he never wants to experience again, the second day of an inquest into death of Newmarket resident 26 year old Evan Arnold. heard.Mr. Arnold was inside a home on Southwind, a small residential road southwest of Leslie and Gorham streets.Positioning himself at the left side of a stone porch of the home, Const. Biersteker peered through a sidelight in the front entrance to spot Mr. Arnold in the foyer, the officer testified while under questioning by coroner's counsel Eric Siebenmorgen.Const. Biersteker noticed a large knife in each of his hands, he said. Mr. Arnold was pacing around inside the home and the officer believed the Newmarket man was "talking himself up" or mentally preparing himself.Before the break-in on Southwind, York police had been searching for Mr. Arnold as part of a sexual assault investigation, the inquest heard Monday.As officers, who had surrounded the home, backed off, Mr. Arnold opened the door and stepped out holding the knives, Const. Biersteker said.The officer drew his gun and pointed it at Mr. Arnold's chest as other officers ordered him to drop the knives.Mr. Arnold said he was going to stab police and had tried to harm himself, the officer testified. "He also stated he was going to take one of us with him," Const. Biersteker said. "These were not threats I had ever heard before."Brandishing the knives, Mr. Arnold went back into the house and began talking to himself and pacing, the officer testified.Mr. Arnold turned around and walked out the door again, this time across the home's lawn, still holding the knives. "He had a purpose," Const. Biersteker said. "He's telling us that he's going to kill us. He turned and locked eyes on me."Mr. Arnold followed Const. Biersteker around a tree and up a slope, the officer testified.As a space behind Mr. Arnold opened, with no fellow officers behind him, Mr. Arnold lunged at Const. Biersteker, the inquest heard."In my estimation, that was him making an attempt to kill me," Const. Biersteker said.He told the inquest he feared for his life and that if he hadn't stopped Mr. Arnold.Const. Biersteker fired twice and struck Mr. Arnold in the chest. Mr. Arnold fell to the ground about eight minutes after Const. Biersteker responded to the call.Mr. Arnold was later pronounced dead at Southlake Regional Health Centre."There is not one single day I haven't thought about it," Const. Biersteker said about shooting Mr. Arnold during cross-examination by police lawyer Joanne Mulcahy. "There was no other option. We're prepared for it, but I hope it never happens again."The shooting was ruled justified by the province's Special Investigations Unit.The inquest will examine the circumstances surrounding Mr. Arnold's death and a three-man, two-woman jury can make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths.Under the Coroner's Act, an inquest is mandatory when a person dies while in custody.During a break in testimony, Mr. Arnold's mother Anne Arnold, who has been granted standing at the inquest - meaning she can play an active role in the proceedings and ask questions - approached Const. Biersteker and clasped his hands.She asked the officer not to burden himself with shooting her son."Please, don't carry it around with you," she told him.The inquest continues.
